common_name: Comtesse Lavinia Maggi Camellia (White-Ground Pink-and-Crimson Striped Formal Double)

planting.note: Blooms open unpredictably variegated from plant to plant and even bloom to bloom, so give it a prominent spot to display the variation.

directions: Comtesse Lavinia Maggi is a formal double Camellia japonica introduced in Italy in 1858, prized for white ground petals irregularly striped, blotched, and flecked with shades of pink, rose, and crimson, so that no two blooms look quite alike and a single plant can even produce solid pink or solid white flowers in the same season. The imbricated, geometrically arranged petals form a dense, symmetric rosette 3 to 4 inches across, opening over a long midseason bloom window from January into March. The shrub grows into a dense, upright, moderately vigorous specimen that has been prized in historic gardens for over a century and a half. Provide filtered shade and consistent moisture on acidic soil to preserve the crispness of its variegated pattern.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry

common_name: Pope Pius IX Camellia (Deep Red 19th-Century Formal Double)

planting.note: A fixture of 19th-century Southern estate gardens, it rewards a sheltered site with filtered shade that protects its dense red petals from sunscald.

directions: 'Pope Pius IX' is a deep red formal double Camellia japonica dating to the mid-19th century, named for the reigning pope of the era and widely distributed through American and European nursery catalogs of the 1850s through 1880s. Its tightly imbricated petals form a symmetric, high-centered rosette 3 to 4 inches across in rich crimson-red, opening over a long midseason display from midwinter into early spring. The upright, compact shrub was a mainstay of 19th-century estate gardens and remains maintained today in historic camellia collections. Grow in dappled shade with acidic, humus-rich soil to keep the dense flower form from browning in direct sun.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry
Historic Southern nursery catalog archives (Fruitland Nurseries)

common_name: Rubescens Major Camellia (Veined Dark Red French Heirloom)

planting.note: Its late bloom window extends camellia color into early spring after most other historic japonicas have already finished.

directions: Rubescens Major is a French heirloom Camellia japonica raised by the Guichard nursery of Nantes and registered in 1866, notable for dark red formal double flowers overlaid with darker crimson veining radiating through each petal. The large, 4 to 5 inch blooms open in a tightly imbricated rosette late in the camellia season, typically February into April, extending color after earlier-blooming cultivars have finished. It forms an unusually vigorous, cold-hardy, upright shrub that has remained in commercial cultivation for more than 150 years. Provide partial shade and well-drained, acidic soil, and expect this variety to tolerate colder winters better than many other 19th-century japonica cultivars.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry

common_name: Lady Hume's Blush Camellia (Historic Blush-Pink Striped Formal Double)

planting.note: One of the first camellias ever grown in Western gardens, it is best sited as a living link to early 19th-century horticultural history.

directions: Lady Hume's Blush ranks among the earliest Camellia japonica cultivars grown in the West, imported to England around 1806 by Sir Abraham Hume and named for his wife. Its pale blush-pink, softly striped petals are arranged in a neat, low-imbricated formal double 2.5 to 3.5 inches across, blooming from midwinter into early spring. Two centuries of continuous cultivation have made it one of the most historically significant camellias in Western gardens, valued today as much for its role in camellia history as for its refined, old-fashioned flower form. Grow in part shade on moist, acidic soil, sheltered from harsh winter wind.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry
Royal Horticultural Society historic plant records

common_name: Paulette Goddard Camellia (Red-and-White Marbled Sport of Adolphe Audusson)

planting.note: Watch for and prune out any branches that revert fully to solid red if strong variegation is the desired look.

directions: 'Paulette Goddard' is a red-and-white variegated sport of the classic 'Adolphe Audusson', introduced by Nuccio's Nurseries of California and named for the mid-20th-century film actress. Its large semi-double to loosely formal double flowers show bold white marbling and streaking over the same deep red ground as its parent cultivar, with blooms occasionally reverting partially or fully to solid red on the same plant. Flowering runs midseason, typically January through March, on a vigorous upright shrub matching the growth habit of its parent. Because variegated sports can be genetically unstable, prune out any fully reverted solid-color branches if a strongly marbled look is desired.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry

common_name: Augusto L. Gouveia Lima Camellia (Giant Lavender-Pink Brazilian Exhibition Camellia)

planting.note: Its outsized blooms can weigh down young branches, so stake or lightly disbud for the best display.

directions: 'Augusto L. Gouveia Lima' is a Brazilian Camellia japonica cultivar prized for producing some of the largest flowers in the species, often 6 inches or more across, in a semi-double to loose peony form of soft lavender-pink to orchid-pink. Introduced into American camellia collections in the 1950s, it quickly became a favorite exhibition and specimen camellia for its combination of enormous bloom size and clear, uniform color. Flowering runs midseason to late season on a vigorous, upright, well-branched shrub. Because its heavy blooms can weigh down thin branches, stake or lightly support young plants and provide filtered light to prevent flower scorch.
sources: American Camellia Society historic cultivar registry
